A membrane aerated biofilm reactor for sulfide control from anaerobically treated
wastewater
Priscila Rosseto Camilotia, Freddy Valdésb, Tiago Palladino Delforno
c, Jan Bartacekd, Marcelo Zaiat
a and
David Jeisone
aBiological Processes Laboratory, Center for Research, Development and Innovation in Environmental Engineering, São Carlos School of
Engineering (EESC), University of São Paulo (USP), São Carlos, SP, Brazil; bNatural Resources Department, Universidad de La Frontera, Temuco,
Chile; cMicrobial Resources Division, Research Center for Chemistry, Biology and Agriculture (CPQBA), Campinas University – UNICAMP,

ABSTRACT
A upflow anaerobic sludge blanket reactor was operated combined to a membrane aerated biofilm
reactor for sulfate removal and for elemental sulfur reclamation. A commercial silicon tube was used
as an oxygen delivery diffuser. The process achieved high rates of sulfide removal from the liquid
phase (90%). The hydrogen sulfide removal was influenced by the pH value and at pH value of 7.5,
98% of the H2S was removed. The elemental sulfur was observed inside the membrane, with
content in the biomass of 21%. Through the massive sequencing of the samples, the microbial
community diversity and the stratification of biomass inside the silicon tube was demonstrated,
confirming the presence of sulfide-oxidizing bacteria on the membrane wall. The most important
genera found related to the sulfur cycle were Sulfuricurvum, Geovibrio, Flexispira and Sulforospirillum.

KEYWORDS
Sulfide oxidation; elemental
sulfur; microaeration; silicon
membrane; high-throughput
sequencing
Highlights
.
Dissolved and gaseous sulfide removal achieved
>90% in microaerobic conditions.
.
Gaseous sulfide removal was influenced by the pH
value; 98% at pH value of 7.5.
.
The elemental sulfur was observed inside the silicone
membrane.
.
Microbial stratification was observed in different
layers inside the membrane.
.
Sulfuricurvum, Geovibrio, Flexispira and Sulforospirillum
were sulfur cycle genera.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic wastewater treatment systems generate waste
streams rich in hydrogen sulfide in the presence of sulfate.
Because their negative impact in many ways, such as a
strong odor, corrosion of steel and concrete structures
and health hazards, waste streams must be treated. The
biogas quality obtained from anaerobic processes is
another example of the need for removing sulfide, as
hydrogen sulfide is very corrosive to some parts of gas
motors and its combustion produces SOx emission.
Hydrogen sulfide could be removed by physicochem-
ical and biological methods. Among the biological
methods, the microaeration has grown, since is reliable,
simple and economically efficient method [1] and con-
sists of applying controlled doses of oxygen in order to
promote the activity of sulfur-oxidizing bacteria (SOB).
The microaeration for sulfide removal has been reported
by Buisman et al. [2] and Jansen et al. [3], and consists of
applying controlled doses of oxygen in order to promote
the activity of SOB.
Tang et al. [4] reported that the kinetics of sulfide
removal by a suspension of SOB biomass confirmed that
the final product of the oxidation of sulfides depends on
the proportion of dissolved oxygen and concentration
of sulfide sulfur. If the oxygen dose is adequately con-
trolled, chemolithotrophic SOB are capable of oxidizing
sulfur compounds to oxidation state 0 and show the feasi-
bility of the treatment while preserving the methane pro-
duction. [5–7]. The microaeration mechanism for sulfide
removal involves the formation of elemental sulfur, an
insoluble intermediate that can be separated from the
liquid phase and reused [8], which represents other
advantage to the treatment process. Krayzelova et al. [1]
summarize in a review paper some methods to use the
microaeration, which refer to controlled dosing of a

small amount of air/oxygen into the liquid or gaseous
phase of anaerobic digesters. The direct air/oxygen injec-
tion in the liquid phase or separated vessels is used in
most reactor configurations [9–12] and the sulfide
removal in the biogas was observed.
The oxygen transfer could be a limiting step during H2S
removal from biogas in microaerobic reactors [13], and a
bubbleless oxygenation could be an alternative to con-
trolledandistheapplicationofmembranestotheaeration.
MABRsareconsidereda newtechnologyforaerobicwaste-
water treatment. Oxygen diffuses through the membrane
into the biofilm where oxidation occurs whereby the
biomass is immobilized on membranes through which
oxygen is supplied. [14]. Using membranes in tubes
offers additional benefits such as a large surface area of
biofilm per unit volume of bioreactor and the ability to
operate at very high flow rates over the biofilm in order
to enhance substrate transfer into the biofilm [15]. Consid-
ering this, a silicone rubber is a potentially efficient means
for supplying oxygen via diffusion through bubbleless gas
transfer. The oxygen is transported through the membrane
and goes directly into the liquid phase in a dissolved form,
because of the high contact time, achieving up to 100% of
oxygen transfers [16]. This characteristic would imply a
minimal oxygen transfer from the liquid phase to biogas,
which results in a great advantage over the direct micro-
aeration in the headspace of the digester, and the tra-
ditional aeration in the liquid phase.
In recent years, there has been increasing interest in
membrane bioreactors for wastewater treatment [17] and
itsusehasbeenreportedfornitrogen removal[18–20],sim-
ultaneous nitrification and organic carbonremoval [21–23].
Using silicon membranes has been also studied in mem-
brane aerated biofilm reactor (MABR) for acetate removal
[15], food processing wastewater [24], phenol [25] and
chlorophenols [26]. Conversely, there is a lack of infor-
mation about the use of this system in sulfide removal.
The aim of this study is to evaluate the feasibility of a
combined upflow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB)–
MABR using silicon membrane for treating sulfate and
sulfide containing wastewater. Moreover, the other
objectives of this study were to explore the sulfide con-
version to sulfur, the influence of the pH value on the dis-
solved and gaseous sulfide removal and analyze the
microbial community structure and function of the domi-
nant species in the biomass inside the membrane.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Bioreactor configuration
The system used in this study was composed of an UASB
reactor connected with a MABR, which consisted of a
silicon membrane inside a chamber. A schematic
diagram of the UASB–MABR system is shown in Figure 1.
The UASB reactor (Figure 1-1) was fed with a flow rate
of 2.1 L d−1. Effluent from the UASB reactor was con-
ducted into the MABR (Figure 1-5) for sequenced biologi-
cal sulfide oxidation. The effluent was circulated through
the silicon membrane by a positive displacement pump
with a flow of 2.7 L h−1.
The silicon membrane (Figure 1-6) was connected
directly to the UASB reactor and was maintained inside a
chamber (Figure 1-5). The chamber was connected to a
bottle, with a working volume of 2.0 L. which was filled
with pure oxygen under constant pressure. The oxygen
stored in the bottle was pumping to the chamber with a
flow of 2.4 L h−1. The bottle was used in the system to
feed the MABR and to allow the gas sampling to observe
biogas diffusion through the membrane.
The UASB reactor has an effective volume of 2.2 L and
was seeded with granular sludge obtained from a full-
scale UASB plant in a brewery (CCU Cervecera, Temuco,
Chile).
The silicon membrane had an internal diameter of
8.0 mm, a wall thickness of 2.4 mm and 2000 mm long. A
single silicon tube was used to allow the biofilm develop-
mentandwasmaintainedthroughoutthereactoroperation
inside a chamber to permit the measure the gas transfer.
2.2. Operational conditions
Three reactors were operated in this study. Two reactors
were operated for 100 days. An UASB reactor was oper-
ated without microaeration for control and the UASB–
MABR system (1) was operated with microaeration. The
UASB–MABR system (2) was also operated for 78 days

reactor system. 1- UASB reactor; 2- feed pump; 3- effluent; 4-

to determine the influence of pH value (pH 7.0 and 7.5).
The temperature was maintained at 30 ± 1°C.
The feed consisted of diluted wine supplemented with
anhydrous sodium sulfate to increase the amount of
sulfide and sodium bicarbonate (10 g L−1). The volumetric
loading rates were approximately 6.0 kgCOD L−1 d−1 and
0.1 kgSO2−
4
L−1 d−1. Sulfur and chemical oxygen demand
(COD) balances were monitored regularly by measuring
the flows of influent and biogas and analyzing liquid and
gas samples. Table 1 summarizes the periods of the study.
The operation of the UASB–MABR system was divided
into three stages. Stage I, before starting the microaera-
tion (day 0–20). Stage II, during the microaeration until
the removal decrease (day 20–49). Stage III, silicon mem-
brane occlusion which was characterized by the sharp
drop in sulfide removal (day 51–109).
2.3. Biofilm start-up
The biofilm start-up took approximately 7 days to
develop the biofilm from inoculation to a visual biofilm
formation. The start-up biofilm growth inside the tube
was encouraged by circulating through membrane
tube synthetic sewage under an organic loading rate of
3.4 kgCOD L−1 d−1. On the second day of operation, a
thin film could be observed on the membrane wall
(MW) and on the sixth day of operation, a black
biomass above the thin film was observed. The rate of
biofilm thickness increase could not be observed due
to system impossibility opening. The biofilm formed
inside the tube was collected at the end of the operation
on the 109th day. Furthermore, the total solids and vola-
tile suspended solids (VSS) were determined.
2.4. Batch tests
The MABR was disconnected from the system on the
92nd day and connected to a bottle to perform batch
experiments in order to observe the capacity of the
anaerobic biofilm layer to reduce the sulfur to sulfide.
The batch experiments were performed in 500 mL
glass bottles filled with 500 mL of basal medium contain-
ing 1 g L−1 of NaHCO3. The bottle was incubated at 30°C
on a shaker at 50 rpm. Ethanol was added after 210 min
(0.5 gCOD L−1) as an electron donor to the sulfur
reduction. Sulfide, sulfate, thiosulfate and COD were
measured in selected time intervals.
2.5. Physical–chemical analysis
Liquid samples were collected from influent and effluent
from the UASB reactors. The sulfate and thiosulfate ions
were analyzed by ionic chromatography (Metrohm,
model 882). Samples were diluted 1:4 with a 0.1 M zinc
acetate solution, followed by centrifugation (5 min at
16,000 g), thus precipitating sulfide as zinc sulfide [27].
The supernatant was filtered at 0.22 µm and the
sample was injected. Sample separation and elution
were performed by an Metrosep A Supp 4 – 250/4.0
analytical column using carbonate/bicarbonate eluent
(4.5 mmol Na2CO3/0.8 mmol NaHCO3 at 1 mL min−1).
Dissolved sulfide was measured by the iodometric
method specified in Standard Methods [28]. Sulfur
content in the sludge and in the biofilm was estimated
from an elemental analysis of sulfur. Samples were
dried at 95°C, cooled and analyzed in an elemental ana-
lyzer (euroEA 3000- Eurovector). COD and VSS were
determined according to standard methods [28]. The
biogas production was measured by liquid displacement
in an inverted cylinder. Biogas composition (O2, N2, CO2,
CH4) was measured by gas chromatography (GC-TCD)
Clarus 580 (PerkinElmer) equipped with a thermal con-
ductivity detector. A Carboxen 1000 (15 ft × 1/8 in ss)
column was used. Helium was the carrier gas. The inlet,
detector and oven temperature were 200°C, 250°C and
120°C, respectively. The H2S in biogas was analyzed
using colorimetric gas detection tubes (RAE system).
The pH values were monitored online using a specific
probe and adjusted by HCl or NaOH (1 M) with a flow
of 0.4 mL min−1.
2.6. Biological analysis by 16s rRNA gene
sequencing
A massive amplicon sequencing of the rRNA 16S on a
Miseq 2 × 250 – Illumina platform, (Illumina Inc., San
Diego, CA, U.S.A.) was carried out to identify the microbial
community in the reactor. Three samples were collected at
the end of reactor operation from MABR to evaluate the
biological diversity in each sample. The samples were col-
lected from three different points: the sample from the
MW; from sulfur formations attached to the MW (SF) and
from the middle of the membrane – the internal
biomass (IB). The sites of sample collection were chosen
based on physical differences noted in the biofilm.
The collected samples were retrieved by successive
washing

using the phenol: chloroform-based protocol described
by [29]. DNA quality was assessed by the 260/280-nm
>1.8, measured by an ND-2000 spectrophotometer
(Nanodrop Inc., Wilmington, DE, U.S.A.). Furthermore,

sis using a primer set that ﬂanked the V3 and V4 hypervari-
able region of the 16S rRNA gene [30]. The full-length
primer sequences, using standard IUPAC nucleotide
nomenclature, to follow the protocol targeting this
region are: 16S Amplicon PCR Forward Primer primers
16S (S-D-Bact-0341-b-S-17) (CCTACGGGNGGCWGCAG)
and 16S Amplicon PCR Reverse Primer S-D-Bact-0785-a-

The sequences were pre-processed using the CASAVA
(1.8.2) Software. Sequences were first trimmed to remove
the adaptor, barcodes, primers and sequences contain-
ing ambiguous ‘N’ or shorter than 200 bps (Software
Seqyclean
(https://bitbucket.org/izhbannikov/seqy-
clean). The minimum read Q score adopted was 24
(Phred Quality). Sequences shorter than 65 bp, or con-
taining ambiguous nucleotides, or with an occurrence
lower or equal to 65 were excluded using the Seqyclean
program. The vector contamination was removed with
the UNIVEC contaminant base (http://www.ncbi.nlm.
nih.gov/VecScreen/UniVec.html).
The alignment of the sequences was performed using
the Pynast tool according to Caporaso et al. [31]. To
determine the operational taxonomic units (OTU), ‘hier-
archical clustering’ was used with 97% similarity. Single-
ton sequences (OTU with one sequence) that may
represent sequencing errors [32] were removed.
For the taxonomic classification of sequences repre-
sentative of each OTUs, the RDP-Classifier was used.
The confidence threshold adopted was 80% for genus
and 50% for other taxonomic levels (Phylum-Family).
Alfa (Chao1, Shannon, Simpson and Dominance) and
Beta (Bray–Curtis dissimilarity index) diversity were quan-
tified using Past software [33]. For this, the dataset was
normalized using the QIIME script [31]. The Circos
diagram [34] was used to compare and visualize the
genus found from the samples.
The sequences generated in this study were deposited
in the European Nucleotide Archive (http://www.ebi.ac.
uk) under project accession number is PRJEB12845.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Performance of the UASB–MABR system
After starting the microaeration until the removal
decrease (stage 2 – day 20–49), the reactor produced a
biogas
with
an
average
of
hydrogen
sulfide
concentration and average removal in the biogas of
377.8 ± 156.3 ppmv and 98%, respectively. The dissolved
sulfide had an average removal and concentration of
90% and 10.9 ± 5.8 mg L−1. During this period, the
hydrogen sulfide concentration was below 400 ppmv
in 8 out 11 samples. The sulfate and COD removal was
stable during the whole operation showing an average
of 69.9 ± 11.8% and 88.0 ± 3.7%, respectively. The dis-
solved sulfide and the sulfide in the biogas concen-
trations in the UASB–MABR system are shown in Figure 1.
Organic matter removal and the methane production
were not significantly affected by microaeration. The
COD removal shows an average of 88.0 ± 3.7% and
85.0 ± 7.6% for the UASB–MABR system and for the
control, respectively. The concentration of methane
and carbon dioxide in the biogas in the UASB–MABR
system showed the same behavior as the control
reactor. The average methane concentration in % (v/v)
was 54.2 ± 14.7 and 52.2 ± 14.4 and the average carbon
dioxide was 34.2 ± 11.7 and 35.7 ± 22.5 for the UASB–
MABR system and the control, respectively. This indicates
that limited oxygen supply did not reduce the energetic
content of the biogas.
The biogas that diffused through the membrane was
analyzed and the sampling was performed on the
chamber. The concentration of the main biogas com-
ponents, methane and carbon dioxide, showed an
average of 23.1 ± 14.9 and 23.2 ± 8.8% (v/v), respectively.
During the biofilm start-up (day 20–27) the sulfide con-
centration in the chamber showed an average of 30.0
± 11.9 mg L−1 and after the biofilm formation the
sulfide concentration was not detected (day 29–65),
demonstrating the biofilm capacity of sulfide removal.
In stage 3 (day 51–109), the concentration of dis-
solved sulfide and sulfide in the biogas increased,
showing an average concentration of 23.9 ± 6.4 mg L−1
and 2560 ± 1030 ppmv (Figure 2). In this phase, the
biofilm became thick, which makes it difficult to transfer
oxygen.
The concept of different layers in the biofilm is
important
to
understand the
performance
of
the
UASB–MABR system. Casey et al. [14] report that in
the conventional biofilms, the active layer is generally
an oxic layer, typically 50–200 mm in thickness, which
corresponds to the depth of oxygen penetration into
the biofilm. If the overall biofilm thickness is greater
than the oxygen penetration depth, then an anoxic
layer, adjacent to the biofilm support, occurs. The
different layers occur in this study. The layer attached
to the inner surface of the membrane was responsible
for the sulfide oxidation; however, the increase in
biofilm thickness may have caused a resistance to the
sulfide reaction with oxygen.

At stage 3, the elemental sulfur reduction to sulfide
could be proved by the batch test with ethanol addition
(Figure 3). It can be observed that there was an increase
in
the
sulfide
concentration
accompanied
by
the

indicating the reduction of sulfur to sulfide. At the begin-
ning of the operation, a concentration of 550 µg L−1 of
sulfide was measured, possibly by the biofilm first
wash. The sulfide concentration has a decrease after
30 min,
with
an
average
concentration
of
59.2 ±
19.5 µg L−1. After 240 min, ethanol was added and the
sulfide concentration showed an increase. The dissolved
oxygen also showed a decrease after 30 min, however,
the concentration showed a slight decrease, probably
by the oxidation of ethanol. The oxygen utilization to
the sulfide or sulfur oxidation did not occur as sulfate
and thiosulfate was not observed.
Similar reactors using immobilized microorganisms
on membranes used to the aeration have also demon-
strated the decline in the efficiency with the biofilm
increase. Pankhania et al. [35] reported a decline in the
COD efficiency in a reactor using hollow fiber and used
the backwash to reduce the biofilm thickness. The
authors
also
concluded
that
the
decline
in
COD
removal efficiency prior to the backwash could be due
to reduced mass transfer as a result of increasing
biofilm thickness or declining biomass activity with
metabolite accumulation in the dense biofilm. Casey
et al. [15] also reported that an optimum biofilm thick-
ness exists, which maximizes the overall reaction rate
by minimizing the diffusional resistance of substrate
and nutrient transfer in sections of the biofilm where bio-
degradation does not take place. Using a tubular silicon
membrane, where the microorganisms grow inside the
membrane, the oxygen mass transfer will occur in the
MW and the active layer to the sulfide conversion is
close to the biofilm–membrane interface. Unless the
biofilm thickness is the same as the thickness of the
active layer, a diffusional resistance to oxygen and
sulfide transfer through the biofilm will occur [15]. In
the present study, the thick biofilm did not completely
penetrate the oxygen and sulfide in the biofilm and
dual limitation predominated. In this case, the optimiz-
ation and stable sulfide removal efficiency can easily be
achieved by backwashing the membrane.
3.2. Sulfur balance
A sulfur balance was performed in order to study the
results of sulfide oxidation and to investigate its conver-
sion to sulfur in the UASB–MABR system. The UASB–
MABR system and reactor control performance data, in
terms of S-containing compounds, are presented in
Table 2. During stage 2, the introduction of oxygen sub-
stantially altered the sulfur outputs of the process. From
the effluent data, it can be observed that the complete
re-oxidation to sulfate did not occur and neither did

3.3. pH effect
The pH effect was also studied simultaneously in
another system for 82 days. The system was also a
UASB–MABR (2) with the same conditions and the
biofilm developed was similar to the other one. The
pH value significantly affects the undissociated H2S
form of sulfide which, by the displacement of the equi-
librium, leads the sulfide from the gas phase to the
liquid phase, which is further treated in the microaero-
bic system. For the pH value of 7.5 (stage 2), the sulfide
concentration in biogas had a maximum removal of
98% and for pH 7.0 (stage 3), the maximum removal
was 50%. Figure 4 shows the average and standard
deviation to dissolve the sulfide and hydrogen sulfide
concentration for each stage.
The microaeration combined with alkaline conditions
was beneficial. While microaeration with air dosed into
the gas phase removed only hydrogen sulfide from
biogas, others studies with injection directly into the
liquid could remove hydrogen sulfide from biogas and
liquid phase. However, the efficiency of hydrogen
removal was not high in this study (stage 3) and others
studies with low concentrations of oxygen [9].
Summary, our findings about the use of the UASB–
MABR for the sulfide conversion to the elemental sulfur
indicate that the oxygen supply through the silicon mem-
brane combined with alkaline pH promote the sulfide
removal both for the liquid and gas phase. Therefore,
the additional step of removing hydrogen sulfide from

3.4. Microbiological analysis
After opening the system, the biofilm could be analyzed
and was observed different layers, which have devel-
oped and differentiated naturally. The biofilm stratifica-
tion could be observed visually. In this way, the
composition of the bacterial community in the three
different layers was studied and showed that different
communities were established throughout the biofilm.
The samples were taken from biomass attached to the
silicon MW, from the elemental sulfur formation in the
membrane (SF) and from the middle of the membrane
(IB). The microorganisms related to the sulfide oxidation
were found attached to the inner surface of the mem-
brane and the sample taken from the middle of the
membrane mostly showed an anaerobic community.
In total, out of the three samples, 76,128–149,693 raw
sequences were generated with an average length of
394 ± 92 bp. During the processing of sequences, 40–
47% of sequences were removed due to the low
quality of the bases (Qphred > 24), lengths less than
200 bp, chimeras or ambiguous bases. The values of cov-
erage estimation (Good’s formula) ranged from 98% to
99%, indicating a high coverage of the diversity.
The analyses of the rarefaction curves were used to
infer that the phylum taxonomic level (80% similarity –
phylum level) and the number of sequences obtained
were sufficient to represent all the diversity in the
biomass (Supplementary Figure 1). However, the rare-
faction curves at 95% (genus level) and 97% (species
level) of similarity showed that more sequence is
necessary to access the full diversity of genera and
species. Furthermore, the richness estimator (Chao 1)
values observed in the MW sample (5057 ± 173) were
higher than those observed in the SF sample (2209 ±
119) and IB sample (832 ± 68). The Shannon diversity
index yielded values greater than 4.0 for all samples,
which shows high diversity (MW: 4.64 ± 0.02; SF: 4.22
± 0.03 and IB: 4.86 ± 0.01).
By using a Bray–Curtis similarity dendrogram (Figure
S1(a)), the similarities among the communities were
determined and show a high similarity (64%) between
the sulfur formation and the sample drawn from the
MW. A similarity of 42% was observed between the
samples taken from the MW (MW and SF) and the
sample drawn from the IB. The clustering of MW
samples may be due to the microaerobic conditions
and the low similarity between the IB sample and the
MW and SF samples indicate the stratification layers of
the biofilm. In addition, the Venn diagram showed that
23% of OTUs were exclusive for the samples taken
from the MW (13% for MW and 10% for SF), while the
IB sample had 7.5% exclusive OTUs (Figure S1(b)).
To understand the microbial community structure
and the biological stratification in the UASB–MABR
system at the three stages, the classified OTUs were
analyzed at phylum and family level (Figure 5). Mean-
while, to explain the key role of the dominant genera,
the classified OTUs were analyzed at the genus level
(Figure 6). The RDP-Classifier was used for the taxo-
nomic classification and showed that over 96% of the
sequences were classified at the phylum level. At the
genera level, the percentage ranged from 53% to
68% of the classified sequences. The main phyla
founded for the samples MW, SF and IB (Figure 5)
were the Proteobacteria (54.1%; 64.9% and 28.5%), Fir-
micutes (7.9%; 8.2% and 24.2%) and the Bacteriodetes
phylum (20.2%; 14.1% and 24.9%).
In total, for the three samples, 19 genera were ident-
ified. The most abundant genus was the Sulfuricurvum
genera. In addition, six other genera related to the
sulfur cycle were found. Two of them are related to oxi-
dation of the sulfide and were exclusively found in
samples withdrawn from the MW, which were Geovibrio
(3.2% for MW and 2.4% for SF), Flexispira (1.2% for MW
and 2.8% for SF) and Sulfurospirillum. (1.1–1.2% for MW
and SF). It is also important to emphasize the role of
sulfate-reducing bacteria, which can be attached to Palu-
dibacter, Desulfovibrio and Desulfobulbus genera and

Figure 6 shows the Circos diagram, which lists the
samples to the genera found in each sample and the rela-
tive abundance. In addition, the genera were divided into
three groups: anaerobic, aerobic and microaerobic.
Among the major genera, Sulfuricurvum genera rep-
resented more than 24.0% and 37.9% (relative abun-
dance) of the MW and SF sample and 16.8% for the IB
sample. The species related to the genera was Sulfuricur-
vum kujiense and was found in the three samples. The
species was described by Kodama and Watanabe [36] as
a facultative anaerobic sulfur-oxidizing bacterium that
grows anaerobically and microaerobically by oxidizing
reduced sulfur species, such as sulfide, elemental sulfur
and thiosulfate, however, under anaerobic conditions,
nitrate can be used as an electron acceptor.
It can also be observed in the Circos diagram that all
the samples are related to the three groups, but
sample MW shows most genera associated to the
anaerobic group. In the anaerobic group, the following
sulfate-reducing bacteria can be observed: Desulfobul-
bus, Desulfovibrio and Paludibacter. Another anaerobic
species with high relative abundance was the Geobacter
lovleyi species. This species was identified in the three
samples, but with greater abundance in the samples

taken from the wall membrane samples. Although
anaerobic species were found in the samples attached
to the membrane, this species can be associated to
using elemental sulfur as an electron acceptor [37],
which reduces sulfur and sulfide production.
The four microaerobic genera found in the greatest
abundance are related to the sulfur cycle. Moreover, Sul-
furicurvum, Geovibrio, Flexispira and Sulforospirillum were
found, and the last three were exclusively found in
samples taken from the MW (MW and SF samples), indi-
cating the stratification and development of the biomass
of different communities. The genus Geovibrio is related
to oxidation of the sulfide [38], although the Flexispira
and Sulforospirillum are associated to the reduction of
elemental sulfur.
Finally, through the massive sequencing of the
samples, the stratification of the biomass inside the
silicon tube was confirmed. The development of microor-
ganisms related to oxidation of sulfide in the MW con-
firms the hypothesis that the mass transfer resistance
may have provided different genera, resulting in differ-
ent layers inside the tube.
4. Conclusions
The dissolved and gaseous sulfide removal achieved, in
microaerobic conditions, efficiency higher than 90%
and 98%, respectively. The gaseous sulfide removal was
influenced by the pH value, at a pH value of 7.5, 98%
of the H2S was removed from biogas and further
treated in the microaerobic reactor. Thus, the oxygen
supply through the silicon membrane combined with
alkaline pH promotes the sulfide removal both for the
liquid and gas phase. The removal efficiency shows a
decrease due to biofilm development, that shows an
additional resistance to the sulfide reaction with the
oxygen. Microorganisms related to the sulfide oxidation
was found attached to the inner surface of the mem-
brane, and the sample taken from the middle of mem-
brane

an
anaerobic
community. Therefore, in the future researches are
required to find practical methods to reduce the
biofilm inside the membrane by increasing the flow
rate or by applying cleaning cycles.
